title: Iran's Araghchi Says Security Breach That Enabled Khamenei Assassination May Still Exist
excerpt: The foreign minister, who survived the same attack that killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, warns the intelligence failure has not been resolved as US strikes enter their second week.
body:
• Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the intelligence breach that allowed the US-Israeli strike on Ayatollah Khamenei’s compound on February 28 “probably still exists.”
  • Araghchi was inside Khamenei’s office when the strike hit and spent two days uncertain of the Supreme Leader’s fate before confirmation of his death.
  • The revelation comes as US forces carry out a seventh consecutive night of strikes on Iran, with the ceasefire fully collapsed and both sides escalating.
  • Iran’s hardliners have accused top officials including Araghchi of staging a “soft coup” by negotiating with Washington against the orders of the new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.

Iran’s top diplomat has made a startling admission: the security failure that allowed the United States and Israel to kill Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei may not have been fixed.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who was inside Khamenei’s office compound when the February 28 strike hit, told Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen television that the intelligence breach that enabled the assassination “probably still exists,” raising questions about the security of Iran’s remaining leadership.

Inside the Strike

Araghchi recounted being in Khamenei’s office at the moment of the attack. “At the moment of his martyrdom, I was in the office that was attacked,” he said. “My first thought and my first concern was the condition of the Leader.”

The foreign minister said he emerged from the rubble and spent two days uncertain about Khamenei’s fate while organizing evacuation efforts. He recalled that the 85-year-old Ayatollah had refused repeated advice to move to a secure location.

“I will not go to a shelter or to a secure location unless every member of the Iranian people also has access to a safe place. Whatever happens to my people will happen to me as well.”

— Ayatollah Khamenei, as recalled by FM Araghchi

Israel subsequently struck a secret bunker beneath Khamenei’s Tehran compound, and a later strike on a nearby building killed eight senior Iranian officials. The Israeli military said more than 300 Iranian ballistic missile launchers — roughly 60% of the country’s total inventory — have been destroyed since the war began.

A Regime Under Pressure

The security admission comes at a fraught moment for Iran’s government. Mojtaba Khamenei, the late Ayatollah’s son and successor as Supreme Leader, has remained hidden from public view since the February 28 attack, which reportedly left him injured.

According to CNN, hardline factions within Iran have accused the country’s visible leadership — including Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian — of staging a “soft coup” against the Islamic Republic. At Khamenei’s funeral in Tehran, mourners pelted Araghchi with rocks, chanting “traitorous sellout,” while others shouted “death to the compromiser” at President Pezeshkian.

Radical lawmaker Mahmoud Nabavian asked on X: “Warning to the people of Iran: Is a coup on the way??”

War Escalates

The internal turmoil coincides with a sharp escalation in fighting. US Central Command confirmed seven consecutive nights of strikes on Iran as of Friday, targeting military logistics, underground weapons storage, and maritime capabilities. More than 50,000 US service members remain deployed across the Middle East.

Iran has expanded its retaliation, striking infrastructure in Kuwait and Qatar, firing at a US base in Syria for the first time, and threatening to close the Red Sea through Houthi proxies. The ceasefire agreement signed in mid-June collapsed on July 7 after disputes over the administration of the Strait of Hormuz.

President Trump dismissed the defunct memorandum of understanding, telling radio host Hugh Hewitt: “It was built to test. It was a test. We didn’t know if it would amount to anything. It didn’t.”

Implications for the Diaspora

The deepening conflict has direct consequences for Indians in the Gulf. India has banned its seafarers from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz after two nationals were killed in regional attacks, and over 15,000 Indian crew members remain stranded. The Dubai economy, home to a large Indian expatriate community, has been hammered by the war, with Indians facing job losses and pay cuts.

Araghchi’s admission that the security breach remains unresolved adds uncertainty to an already volatile situation. If Iran’s own leadership cannot be confident in its security apparatus, the prospect of a stable resolution to the war grows more distant.
